MOLECULAR GENETICS LABORATORY REPORT
[redacted location] Medical Center
Department of Medical Genetics

PATIENT INFORMATION
Name: [redacted name]
Date of Birth: [redacted date]
Medical Record Number: [redacted ID]
Specimen Type: Peripheral blood
Date Collected: [redacted date]
Date Received: [redacted date]
Date Reported: [redacted date]

REFERRAL REASON
Diagnostic testing for Fragile X syndrome

CLINICAL INDICATION
Pediatric patient referred for molecular genetic testing to evaluate for Fragile X syndrome.

METHODOLOGY
FRAXA Analysis (FMR1 gene):
- PCR amplification of the CGG repeat region in the FMR1 gene promoter
- Southern blot analysis using probe StB12.3 to detect expanded alleles
- Methylation-sensitive restriction enzyme digestion to assess methylation status

FRAXE Analysis (FMR2 gene):
- PCR amplification of the GCC repeat region in the FMR2 gene
- Fragment analysis by capillary electrophoresis

RESULTS

FRAXA (FMR1) Analysis:
Allele 1: 29 CGG repeats
Allele 2: 31 CGG repeats
Methylation Status: Normal pattern
Interpretation: NORMAL - Both alleles are within the normal range

FRAXE (FMR2) Analysis:
Allele 1: 16 GCC repeats
Allele 2: 18 GCC repeats
Interpretation: NORMAL - Both alleles are within the normal range

SUMMARY
Molecular genetic testing for FRAXA and FRAXE expansion mutations shows normal results. Both FMR1 and FMR2 allele sizes are within the normal range. These findings significantly reduce the likelihood of Fragile X syndrome to less than 1%.

TECHNICAL NOTES
Reference Ranges:
FMR1 (FRAXA):
- Normal: 5-44 CGG repeats
- Intermediate: 45-54 CGG repeats
- Premutation: 55-200 CGG repeats
- Full mutation: >200 CGG repeats

FMR2 (FRAXE):
- Normal: 6-35 GCC repeats
- Intermediate: 36-60 GCC repeats
- Full mutation: >200 GCC repeats

LIMITATIONS
This assay detects CGG/GCC repeat expansions in the FMR1 and FMR2 genes. Rare cases of Fragile X syndrome may result from point mutations, deletions, or other rearrangements within the FMR1 gene that would not be detected by this method. If clinical suspicion remains high, additional testing such as FMR1 gene sequencing may be considered.

REPORTED BY
[redacted name], PhD, FACMG
Laboratory Director

This test was developed and its performance characteristics determined by [redacted location] Medical Center Molecular Genetics Laboratory. It has not been cleared or approved by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration.
